claim: Müllerian mimicry is a positive interspecific interaction, whereby co-occurring defended prey species share a common aposematic signal.
source: Müllerian mimicry is a positive interspecific interaction, whereby co-occurring defended prey species share a common aposematic signal.
evidence: This is a definitional statement that draws from established scientific knowledge about Müllerian mimicry.

claim: In Lepidoptera, aposematic species typically harbour conspicuous opaque wing colour patterns with convergent optical properties among co-mimetic species.
source: In Lepidoptera, aposematic species typically harbour conspicuous opaque wing colour patterns with convergent optical properties among co-mimetic species.
evidence: This statement draws from established knowledge about aposematic Lepidoptera and is supported by the context of the study.

claim: Some aposematic mimetic species have partially transparent wings.
source: Surprisingly, some aposematic mimetic species have partially transparent wings, raising the questions of whether optical properties of transparent patches are also convergent, and of how transparency is achieved.
evidence: This is an observation that motivates the study and is supported by the species examined in the manuscript.

claim: Transparency, as perceived by predators, is convergent among co-mimics in some mimicry rings.
source: We show that transparency, as perceived by predators, is convergent among co-mimics in some mimicry rings.
evidence: This claim is supported by the spectrophotometry measurements and bird vision modeling analyses presented in the results.

claim: Underlying micro- and nanostructures are sometimes convergent despite a large structural diversity.
source: Underlying micro- and nanostructures are also sometimes convergent despite a large structural diversity.
evidence: This is supported by the SEM imaging and comparative analyses of structural features across species.

claim: Transparency is primarily produced by microstructure modifications.
source: We reveal that while transparency is primarily produced by microstructure modifications, nanostructures largely influence light transmission, potentially enabling additional fine-tuning in transmission properties.
evidence: This is supported by the PGLS analyses linking structural features to mean transmittance.

claim: Nanostructures largely influence light transmission, potentially enabling additional fine-tuning in transmission properties.
source: We reveal that while transparency is primarily produced by microstructure modifications, nanostructures largely influence light transmission, potentially enabling additional fine-tuning in transmission properties.
evidence: This is supported by the PGLS analyses showing the effect of nanostructure density on mean transmittance.

claim: Transparency might not only enable camouflage but can also be part of aposematic signals.
source: This study shows that transparency might not only enable camouflage but can also be part of aposematic signals.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the convergence of transparency among co-mimetic species.

claim: Lepidoptera are characterised by large wings typically covered by scales.
source: Lepidoptera (butterflies and moths) are characterised by large wings typically covered by scales, as testified by the name of the order (after the ancient greek lepís - scale and pterón – wing).
evidence: This is established knowledge about Lepidoptera morphology.

claim: Scales can contain pigments or generate structural colours, thereby producing colour patterns across the entire wing.
source: Scales can contain pigments or generate structural colours, thereby producing colour patterns across the entire wing.
evidence: This is established knowledge about how Lepidoptera wing coloration is produced.

claim: Wing colour patterns are involved in thermoregulation.
source: Wing colour patterns are involved in thermoregulation (Dufour et al., 2018; Heidrich et al., 2018), sexual selection (Kemp, 2007), and anti-predator defences, such as crypsis (Cook et al., 2012; Endler, 1984; Webster et al., 2009), masquerade (Skelhorn et al., 2010; Stoddard, 2012), disruptive coloration, and deflection of predator attacks (Vallin et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Wing colour patterns are involved in sexual selection.
source: Wing colour patterns are involved in thermoregulation (Dufour et al., 2018; Heidrich et al., 2018), sexual selection (Kemp, 2007), and anti-predator defences, such as crypsis (Cook et al., 2012; Endler, 1984; Webster et al., 2009), masquerade (Skelhorn et al., 2010; Stoddard, 2012), disruptive coloration, and deflection of predator attacks (Vallin et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Wing colour patterns are involved in anti-predator defences, such as crypsis.
source: Wing colour patterns are involved in thermoregulation (Dufour et al., 2018; Heidrich et al., 2018), sexual selection (Kemp, 2007), and anti-predator defences, such as crypsis (Cook et al., 2012; Endler, 1984; Webster et al., 2009), masquerade (Skelhorn et al., 2010; Stoddard, 2012), disruptive coloration, and deflection of predator attacks (Vallin et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Wing colour patterns are involved in masquerade.
source: Wing colour patterns are involved in thermoregulation (Dufour et al., 2018; Heidrich et al., 2018), sexual selection (Kemp, 2007), and anti-predator defences, such as crypsis (Cook et al., 2012; Endler, 1984; Webster et al., 2009), masquerade (Skelhorn et al., 2010; Stoddard, 2012), disruptive coloration, and deflection of predator attacks (Vallin et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Wing colour patterns are involved in deflection of predator attacks.
source: Wing colour patterns are involved in thermoregulation (Dufour et al., 2018; Heidrich et al., 2018), sexual selection (Kemp, 2007), and anti-predator defences, such as crypsis (Cook et al., 2012; Endler, 1984; Webster et al., 2009), masquerade (Skelhorn et al., 2010; Stoddard, 2012), disruptive coloration, and deflection of predator attacks (Vallin et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Aposematism involves advertising the presence of secondary defences by means of bright and contrasted colour patterns.
source: Another type of anti-predator defence in Lepidoptera involving wing colour pattern is aposematism, where the presence of secondary defences is advertised by the means of bright and contrasted colour patterns.
evidence: This is established knowledge about aposematism.

claim: Aposematic species often engage in Müllerian mimetic interactions because of positive frequency-dependent selection incurred on aposematic signals.
source: Because of the positive frequency-dependent selection incurred on aposematic signals (Greenwood and Cotton, 1989, Chouteau et al., 2016), aposematic species often engage in Müllerian mimetic interactions, whereby species exposed to the same suite of predators converge on the same colour pattern and form mimicry 'rings' (Müller, 1879).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Co-mimetic species are often distantly related, implying multiple independent evolution of the same colour pattern.
source: Co-mimetic species (species that share a common aposematic colour pattern) are often distantly related, implying multiple independent evolution of the same colour pattern.
evidence: This is established knowledge about mimicry systems.

claim: Among co-mimetic lepidopteran species, analogous colour patches cannot be discriminated by birds.
source: Among such co-mimetic lepidopteran species, several studies using visual modelling have shown that analogous colour patches (i. e. those occupying a similar position in the wing and harbouring similar colour) cannot be discriminated by birds, believed to be the main predators (Bybee et al., 2012; Llaurens et al., 2014; Su et al., 2015; Thurman and Seymoure, 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Birds are believed to be the main predators of Lepidoptera.
source: Among such co-mimetic lepidopteran species, several studies using visual modelling have shown that analogous colour patches (i. e. those occupying a similar position in the wing and harbouring similar colour) cannot be discriminated by birds, believed to be the main predators (Bybee et al., 2012; Llaurens et al., 2014; Su et al., 2015; Thurman and Seymoure, 2016).
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field, supported by citations.

claim: Mimicry selects for convergent or advergent colourations, as perceived by predators.
source: Therefore, mimicry selects for convergent (when a trait in different species evolves towards the same value) or advergent (when a trait of a given species evolves towards the trait value in another species) colourations, as perceived by predators.
evidence: This is an inference based on the cited studies and established theory of mimicry.

claim: Some unpalatable, aposematic species exhibit transparent wing patches.
source: Surprisingly, although most aposematic Lepidoptera species harbour brightly coloured patterns, some unpalatable (due to the presence of chemical compounds in their body), aposematic species exhibit transparent wing patches (McClure et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: In tropical America, many mimicry rings comprise transparent species.
source: Notably, in tropical America, many mimicry rings comprise such transparent species (Beccaloni, 1997; Elias et al., 2008; Willmott et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Scales can fall upon adult emergence as a means to achieve transparency.
source: Previous studies on a handful of species (most of which are not aposematic) have revealed several, non-mutually exclusive means to achieve transparency, through scale modification or scale shedding, with the effect of reducing the total coverage of the chitin membrane by scales. Scales can fall upon adult emergence (Yoshida et al., 1996); they can have a reduced size (Dushkina et al., 2017; Goodwyn et al., 2009) and even resemble bristle (Binetti et al., 2009; Hernández-Chavarría et al., 2004; Goodwyn et al., 2009; Siddique et al., 2015); they can be either flat on the membrane (Goodwyn et al., 2009) or erected (Dushkina et al., 2017; Goodwyn et al., 2009), which also reduces effective membrane coverage by scales.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: Scales can have a reduced size as a means to achieve transparency.
source: Previous studies on a handful of species (most of which are not aposematic) have revealed several, non-mutually exclusive means to achieve transparency, through scale modification or scale shedding, with the effect of reducing the total coverage of the chitin membrane by scales. Scales can fall upon adult emergence (Yoshida et al., 1996); they can have a reduced size (Dushkina et al., 2017; Goodwyn et al., 2009) and even resemble bristle (Binetti et al., 2009; Hernández-Chavarría et al., 2004; Goodwyn et al., 2009; Siddique et al., 2015); they can be either flat on the membrane (Goodwyn et al., 2009) or erected (Dushkina et al., 2017; Goodwyn et al., 2009), which also reduces effective membrane coverage by scales.
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Scales can resemble bristle as a means to achieve transparency.
source: Previous studies on a handful of species (most of which are not aposematic) have revealed several, non-mutually exclusive means to achieve transparency, through scale modification or scale shedding, with the effect of reducing the total coverage of the chitin membrane by scales. Scales can fall upon adult emergence (Yoshida et al., 1996); they can have a reduced size (Dushkina et al., 2017; Goodwyn et al., 2009) and even resemble bristle (Binetti et al., 2009; Hernández-Chavarría et al., 2004; Goodwyn et al., 2009; Siddique et al., 2015); they can be either flat on the membrane (Goodwyn et al., 2009) or erected (Dushkina et al., 2017; Goodwyn et al., 2009), which also reduces effective membrane coverage by scales.
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Scales can be flat on the membrane or erected, which reduces effective membrane coverage by scales.
source: Previous studies on a handful of species (most of which are not aposematic) have revealed several, non-mutually exclusive means to achieve transparency, through scale modification or scale shedding, with the effect of reducing the total coverage of the chitin membrane by scales. Scales can fall upon adult emergence (Yoshida et al., 1996); they can have a reduced size (Dushkina et al., 2017; Goodwyn et al., 2009) and even resemble bristle (Binetti et al., 2009; Hernández-Chavarría et al., 2004; Goodwyn et al., 2009; Siddique et al., 2015); they can be either flat on the membrane (Goodwyn et al., 2009) or erected (Dushkina et al., 2017; Goodwyn et al., 2009), which also reduces effective membrane coverage by scales.
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Reducing scale density could make wings transparent to some extent.
source: Reducing scale density could also make wings transparent to some extent (Goodwyn et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: Some Lepidoptera achieve transparency with transparent scales.
source: Recently, Gomez et al., 2021 reported that some Lepidoptera achieve transparency with transparent scales.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: Nanostructures on the surface of the wing membrane may enhance transparency through the reduction of light reflection.
source: In addition to scale modifications, the presence of nanostructures on the surface of the wing membrane may enhance transparency through the reduction of light reflection, by generating a gradient of refractive index between the chitin-made membrane and the air allowing better penetration of light through the membrane (Binetti et al., 2009; Siddique et al., 2015; Yoshida et al., 1997).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: The study investigated 62 Neotropical Lepidoptera species belonging to seven families and representing 10 distinct mimicry rings.
source: Here, we investigate the transmission properties and the structural bases of wing transparency in a community of 62 Neotropical Lepidoptera species belonging to seven families and representing 10 distinct mimicry rings.
evidence: This describes the dataset used in the study.

claim: All mimicry rings contain species with transparent wings.
source: All mimicry rings contain species with transparent wings, but in a few of them some co-mimics have opaque wings, or nearly so (see Figure 5—figure supplement 1 for the illustration of this transparency gradient).
evidence: This is supported by the data and Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: In some mimicry rings, some co-mimics have opaque wings, or nearly so.
source: All mimicry rings contain species with transparent wings, but in a few of them some co-mimics have opaque wings, or nearly so (see Figure 5—figure supplement 1 for the illustration of this transparency gradient).
evidence: This is supported by the data and Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: For three spots out of five and across all mimicry rings, the difference in achromatic contrast (dL) between co-mimetic species is significantly smaller than expected both at random and given the phylogenetic distances between species.
source: The results presented in Figure 1 show that for three spots out of five and across all mimicry rings the difference in achromatic contrast (dL) between co-mimetic species is significantly smaller than expected both at random and given the phylogenetic distances between species (Figure 1B), irrespective of the illuminating light or the visual system considered (see Supplementary file 1a and b for results under the full range of conditions).
evidence: This is supported by the statistical analyses and Figure 1.

claim: Differences in chromatic contrasts (dS) between co-mimetic species are marginally significantly smaller than expected at random and given the phylogenetic distance between species only for the most proximal spot on the forewing.
source: Differences in chromatic contrasts (dS) between co-mimetic species are marginally significantly smaller than expected at random and given the phylogenetic distance between species only for the most proximal spot on the forewing (see Supplementary file 1b).
evidence: This is supported by the statistical analyses presented in Supplementary file 1b.

claim: Predators see transparent patches among co-mimetic species as more similar than among species that belong to different mimicry rings.
source: These results mean that, on average, predators see transparent patches among co-mimetic species as more similar than among species that belong to different mimicry rings.
evidence: This is an inference from the statistical analyses of achromatic and chromatic contrasts.

claim: The similarity in transparent patches is due to convergent evolution.
source: The fact that these tests remain significant (dL) or marginally so (dS) with the phylogenetic correction indicates that such similarity in transparent patches is due to convergent evolution.
evidence: This is an inference from the phylogenetically corrected statistical tests.

claim: In six out of 10 mimicry rings, achromatic contrasts (dL) between co-mimetic species are smaller than expected at random for at least one spot on the forewing.
source: When looking more precisely at similarity between co-mimetic species for each individual mimicry ring (Figure 1C), we show that in six out of 10 mimicry rings achromatic contrasts (dL) between co-mimetic species are smaller than expected at random for at least one spot on the forewing (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by the statistical analyses and Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: After accounting for the phylogeny, two out of 10 mimicry rings show achromatic contrasts (dL) between co-mimetic species smaller than expected.
source: After accounting for the phylogeny, this figure drops down to two out of 10 mimicry rings (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by the phylogenetically corrected statistical analyses and Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Six mimicry rings out of 10 comprise co-mimetic species exhibiting smaller chromatic contrast than expected at random.
source: Regarding chromatic contrasts (dS), six mimicry rings out of 10 comprise co-mimetic species exhibiting smaller chromatic contrast than expected at random and three out of them comprise co-mimetic species with smaller chromatic contrast than expected given the phylogeny (Figure 1C, Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by the statistical analyses and Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: Three mimicry rings out of 10 comprise co-mimetic species with smaller chromatic contrast than expected given the phylogeny.
source: Regarding chromatic contrasts (dS), six mimicry rings out of 10 comprise co-mimetic species exhibiting smaller chromatic contrast than expected at random and three out of them comprise co-mimetic species with smaller chromatic contrast than expected given the phylogeny (Figure 1C, Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by the phylogenetically corrected statistical analyses and Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: For some mimicry rings (notably 'theudelinda', 'hewitsoni', 'panthyale'), similarity in transparent patches could be due to shared ancestry.
source: These results suggest that in some cases the similarity in transparent patches between co-mimetic species is due to convergent evolution but we cannot rule out that for some mimicry rings (notably 'theudelinda', 'hewitsoni', 'panthyale') similarity could be due to shared ancestry.
evidence: This is an inference from the phylogenetically corrected statistical tests.

claim: Achromatic aspects (achromatic contrast dL) appear more significant than chromatic aspects (chromatic contrast dS).
source: Achromatic aspects (achromatic contrast dL) appear more significant than chromatic aspects (chromatic contrast dS) (Figure 1, Supplementary file 1a,b), suggesting that selection may act more on broadband transmittance (which is related to the degree of transparency) than on colour in transparent patches.
evidence: This is an inference from the statistical analyses presented in Figure 1 and Supplementary file 1a,b.

claim: Selection may act more on broadband transmittance (which is related to the degree of transparency) than on colour in transparent patches.
source: Achromatic aspects (achromatic contrast dL) appear more significant than chromatic aspects (chromatic contrast dS) (Figure 1, Supplementary file 1a,b), suggesting that selection may act more on broadband transmittance (which is related to the degree of transparency) than on colour in transparent patches.
evidence: This is an inference from the comparative significance of achromatic vs chromatic contrasts.

claim: Scales in transparent patches could be coloured (76% of species) or transparent (24%).
source: Scales could be coloured (76 % of species) or transparent (24%); they could be flat on the membrane (16%) or erected (84%).
evidence: This is supported by the microscopy observations across the 62 species.

claim: Scales could be flat on the membrane (16%) or erected (84%).
source: Scales could be coloured (76 % of species) or transparent (24%); they could be flat on the membrane (16%) or erected (84%).
evidence: This is supported by the microscopy observations across the 62 species.

claim: Scales could be lamellar (55% of species), or piliform (45%).
source: Scales could be lamellar (55 % of species), or piliform (45%).
evidence: This is supported by the microscopy observations across the 62 species.

claim: Piliform scales (mainly bifid) appeared to be almost exclusively found in the Ithomiini tribe.
source: In our dataset, piliform scales (mainly bifid) appeared to be almost exclusively found in the Ithomiini tribe, although one erebid species also harboured monofid piliform scales (Figure 3).
evidence: This is supported by the microscopy observations and phylogenetic mapping shown in Figure 3.

claim: One erebid species harboured monofid piliform scales.
source: In our dataset, piliform scales (mainly bifid) appeared to be almost exclusively found in the Ithomiini tribe, although one erebid species also harboured monofid piliform scales (Figure 3).
evidence: This is supported by the microscopy observations shown in Figure 3.

claim: Five types of nanostructures were found: absent (10% of species), maze (3%), nipple arrays (55%), pillars (21%), and sponge-like (11%).
source: In our sample, we found five types of nanostructures: absent (10 % of species), maze (3%), nipple arrays (55%), pillars (21%), and sponge-like (11%).
evidence: This is supported by the SEM imaging observations across the 62 species.

claim: Both micro- and nanostructure features are highly conserved in the phylogeny.
source: Phylogenetic signal tests show that both micro- and nanostructure features are highly conserved in the phylogeny (Figure 3, Supplementary file 1c), suggesting the existence of constraints in the developmental pathways underlying micro- and nanostructures.
evidence: This is supported by the phylogenetic signal tests presented in Supplementary file 1c and Figure 3.

claim: The existence of constraints in the developmental pathways underlying micro- and nanostructures is suggested by the high phylogenetic conservation of these features.
source: Phylogenetic signal tests show that both micro- and nanostructure features are highly conserved in the phylogeny (Figure 3, Supplementary file 1c), suggesting the existence of constraints in the developmental pathways underlying micro- and nanostructures.
evidence: This is an inference from the phylogenetic signal tests.

claim: The phylogenetic signal is stronger for scale type than for nanostructures.
source: However, the value of δ, the metric used to quantify phylogenetic signal of traits with discrete states (Borges et al., 2019), is higher for scale type than for nanostructures. This means that the phylogenetic signal is stronger for scale type than for nanostructures.
evidence: This is supported by the δ values calculated from the phylogenetic signal tests.

claim: In the nymphalid tribe Ithomiini, microstructures seem to be more conserved than nanostructures.
source: Moreover, in the nymphalid tribe Ithomiini, which is highly represented in our dataset, microstructures seem to be more conserved (all species but the basal species M. curvifascia have piliform scales in transparent patches) than nanostructures (all five types of nanostructures, mixed in the Ithomiini clade, Figure 3).
evidence: This is supported by the observations shown in Figure 3.

claim: Across all mimicry rings, co-mimetic species share structural features more than expected at random and given the phylogeny.
source: We show that, across all mimicry rings, co-mimetic species share structural features (either scale type, nanostructure type, nanostructure density or structural syndrome, defined as the association of scale type and nanostructure type) more than expected at random and given the phylogeny (Figure 4).
evidence: This is supported by the statistical analyses presented in Figure 4.

claim: Structural features are globally convergent between co-mimetic species.
source: The fact that the tests remain significant when phylogenetic correction is applied means that structural features are globally convergent between co-mimetic species.
evidence: This is an inference from the phylogenetically corrected statistical tests.

claim: Microstructures are convergent for 'agnosia' mimicry ring, where species mainly have erected scales.
source: We tested for convergence of structural features in each individual mimicry ring separately (Figure 4D and Figure 4—figure supplement 1) and we found that microstructures are convergent for 'agnosia' mimicry ring, where species mainly have erected scales.
evidence: This is supported by the statistical analyses presented in Figure 4D and Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: In 'panthyale' and 'theudelinda' mimicry rings, species all have similar piliform scales but this similarity is likely due to shared ancestry and not to convergence.
source: In other mimicry rings ('panthyale' and 'theudelinda'), species all have similar piliform scales but this similarity is likely due to shared ancestry and not to convergence.
evidence: This is an inference from the phylogenetically corrected statistical tests.

claim: Nanostructural type showed convergent evolution for 'agnosia' and 'panthyale' mimicry rings.
source: Regarding nanostructural type we revealed convergent evolution for 'agnosia', and 'panthyale' mimicry rings, characterised by nipples and by pillars, respectively (Figure 4D, Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by the statistical analyses presented in Figure 4D and Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Nanostructure density is convergent for 'agnosia', 'confusa', and 'lerida' mimicry rings.
source: Moreover, we showed that nanostructure density is convergent for 'agnosia', 'confusa', and 'lerida' mimicry rings and that it is more similar than expected at random for 'theudelinda' mimicry ring (Figure 4D, Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by the statistical analyses presented in Figure 4D and Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Nanostructure density is more similar than expected at random for 'theudelinda' mimicry ring.
source: Moreover, we showed that nanostructure density is convergent for 'agnosia', 'confusa', and 'lerida' mimicry rings and that it is more similar than expected at random for 'theudelinda' mimicry ring (Figure 4D, Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by the statistical analyses presented in Figure 4D and Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Structural syndrome (association between micro- and nanostructures) is convergent for 'agnosia', where 71% of species harbour a combination of erected scales and nipples.
source: We showed convergence in structural syndrome (association between micro- and nanostructures) for 'agnosia', where 71 % of species harbour a combination of erected scales and nipples (Figure 4D, Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by the statistical analyses presented in Figure 4D and Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: For the mimicry rings 'panthyale' and 'theudelinda', 100% and 80% of species harbour a combination of piliform scales and pillars, respectively, but this similarity is best explained by shared ancestry.
source: For the mimicry rings 'panthyale' and 'theudelinda' 100% and 80% of species harbour a combination of piliform scales and pillars, respectively (Figure 4), but this similarity is best explained by shared ancestry.
evidence: This is an inference from the phylogenetically corrected statistical tests and Figure 4.

claim: Mean transmittance depends mainly on scale type, scale density and nanostructure density.
source: Mean transmittance depends mainly on scale type, scale density and nanostructure density, and to a lesser extent on membrane thickness and scale colour (Figure 5A, Supplementary file 1e).
evidence: This is supported by the PGLS analyses presented in Figure 5A and Supplementary file 1e.

claim: Mean transmittance depends to a lesser extent on membrane thickness and scale colour.
source: Mean transmittance depends mainly on scale type, scale density and nanostructure density, and to a lesser extent on membrane thickness and scale colour (Figure 5A, Supplementary file 1e).
evidence: This is supported by the PGLS analyses presented in Figure 5A and Supplementary file 1e.

claim: Wings covered with piliform scales transmit more light than those covered with lamellar scales.
source: The effect of scale type is retained in all eight models and is significant in all of them. Wings covered with piliform scales transmit more light than those covered with lamellar scales (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is supported by the PGLS analyses and Figure 5B.

claim: Among wings covered with lamellar scales, those with erected scales transmit more light than those with flat scales.
source: Among wings covered with lamellar scales, those with erected scales transmit more light than those with flat scales.
evidence: This is supported by the PGLS analyses.

claim: Mean transmittance decreases as scale density increases.
source: The effect of scale density is retained in the eight best models and is significant in five of those (Supplementary file 1e): mean transmittance decreases as scale density increases.
evidence: This is supported by the PGLS analyses presented in Supplementary file 1e.

claim: Mean transmittance increases when nanostructure density increases.
source: The effect of nanostructure density is retained in six models and is significant in four of those: mean transmittance increases when nanostructure density increases (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is supported by the PGLS analyses and Figure 5C.

claim: The increase in light transmission due to the increase in nanostructure density is not as strong when scale density is high than when scale density is low.
source: The interaction between scale density and nanostructure density is retained in three out of eight models and it is marginally significantly different from zero in two of those three models (Supplementary file 1e). The coefficient is always negative, meaning that the increase in light transmission due to the increase in nanostructure density is not as strong when scale density is high than when scale density is low.
evidence: This is supported by the PGLS analyses presented in Supplementary file 1e.

claim: The contribution of nanostructures to transparency is stronger when scale density is low.
source: This suggests that the contribution of nanostructures to transparency is stronger when scale density is low.
evidence: This is an inference from the interaction between scale density and nanostructure density in the PGLS models.

claim: Light transmission decreases when membrane thickness increases.
source: The effect of membrane thickness is retained in three out of eight models and is significantly different from zero in one of them: light transmission decreases when membrane thickness increases.
evidence: This is supported by the PGLS analyses presented in Supplementary file 1e.

claim: Transparent scales, which do not contain pigments, transmit more light than coloured ones, which contain pigments.
source: Transparent scales, which do not contain pigments, transmit more light than coloured ones, which contain pigments; a relationship which is retained in three out of eight models and is marginally significantly different from zero in one model (Supplementary file 1e).
evidence: This is supported by the PGLS analyses presented in Supplementary file 1e.

claim: Transparent patches in co-mimetic species can be under selection for convergence.
source: Based on bird vision modelling applied to light transmission measurements, we showed that predators see transparent patches of species belonging to the same mimicry ring as more similar than expected at random, and given the phylogeny. Even though this result does not hold for each mimicry ring considered is this study, likely because of a lack of statistical power and/or because some mimicry rings comprise only closely related species, our results suggest that transparent patches in co-mimetic species can be under selection for convergence, mirroring what has been shown for coloured patches in opaque species (Bybee et al., 2012; Llaurens et al., 2014; Su et al., 2015; Thurman and Seymoure, 2016).
evidence: This is an inference from the statistical analyses and comparison with cited literature.

claim: Transparent patches might be part of the aposematic signal.
source: This convergent resemblance, which regards mainly the degree of transparency (a general term to refer to what extent a patch appears transparent), suggests that transparent patches might be part of the aposematic signal.
evidence: This is an inference from the convergence of transparency among co-mimetic species.

claim: Convergence in properties of transparent patches may also result from selection for crypsis.
source: Nevertheless, convergence in properties of transparent patches may also result from other selective processes. Transparency is also involved in crypsis (Arias et al., 2020b), even in aposematic prey (Arias et al., 2019; McClure et al., 2019), and the degree of transparency needed to achieve crypsis may depend on the ambient light (Johnsen and Widder, 1998; Arias et al., 2020a).
evidence: This is speculation supported by citations to published literature.

claim: In bright environments only highly transparent prey are cryptic, whereas in darker environments moderately transparent prey can be cryptic.
source: Specifically, in bright environments only highly transparent prey are cryptic, whereas in darker environments moderately transparent prey can be cryptic.
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Co-mimetic species share their habitat and microhabitat.
source: In our case, as co-mimetic species share their habitat (Chazot et al., 2014) and microhabitat (Willmott et al., 2017), characterised by a specific ambient light, we cannot rule out that the similarity in the degree of transparency observed between co-mimetic species is the result of selection for crypsis rather than aposematism.
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Multiple mimicry rings usually coexist in the same localities.
source: However, several studies on Ithomiini butterflies have shown that multiple mimicry rings usually coexist in the same localities (Beccaloni, 1997; Chazot et al., 2014; Elias et al., 2008; Willmott et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: The species belonging to the mimicry rings 'banjana-m', 'panthyale', 'hewitsoni', and 'theudelinda' are all high-altitude species that are found in the same localities.
source: For example, the species belonging to the mimicry rings 'banjana-m', 'panthyale', 'hewitsoni', and 'theudelinda' are all high-altitude species that are found in the same localities, and are therefore exposed to the same environmental conditions (ambient light, temperature, humidity).
evidence: This is based on knowledge of the species' distributions.

claim: Co-occurring chemically defended species that belong to different mimicry rings differ in transmission properties of their transparent patches.
source: The fact that co-occurring chemically defended species that belong to different mimicry rings differ in transmission properties of their transparent patches (Figure 1—figure supplement 3) suggests that the convergence observed is likely driven by Müllerian mimicry, and is not only the result of selection for crypsis or local adaptation to abiotic factors.
evidence: This is an inference from the data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claim: The convergence observed is likely driven by Müllerian mimicry, and is not only the result of selection for crypsis or local adaptation to abiotic factors.
source: The fact that co-occurring chemically defended species that belong to different mimicry rings differ in transmission properties of their transparent patches (Figure 1—figure supplement 3) suggests that the convergence observed is likely driven by Müllerian mimicry, and is not only the result of selection for crypsis or local adaptation to abiotic factors.
evidence: This is an inference from the observation that co-occurring species in different mimicry rings differ in transparency.

claim: Transparency has been shown to be involved in camouflage and to decrease detectability by predators.
source: This study therefore challenges our vision of transparency, which might have evolved under multiple selective pressures in aposematic butterflies. Transparency has been shown to be involved in camouflage and to decrease detectability by predators (Arias et al., 2020b), even in aposematic species (Arias et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Transparent aposematic Lepidoptera benefit from a double protection from predation, which can act at different distances.
source: Therefore, transparent aposematic Lepidoptera benefit from a double protection from predation, which can act at different distances (Barnett et al., 2018; Cuthill, 2019; Tullberg et al., 2005): transparent aposematic species are less detectable than opaque species (McClure et al., 2019), but when detected they may be recognized as unpalatable by experienced predators, due to their aposematic wing pattern, and spared by those predators.
evidence: This is an inference supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Transparent aposematic species are less detectable than opaque species.
source: Therefore, transparent aposematic Lepidoptera benefit from a double protection from predation, which can act at different distances (Barnett et al., 2018; Cuthill, 2019; Tullberg et al., 2005): transparent aposematic species are less detectable than opaque species (McClure et al., 2019), but when detected they may be recognized as unpalatable by experienced predators, due to their aposematic wing pattern, and spared by those predators.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: When detected, transparent aposematic species may be recognized as unpalatable by experienced predators and spared.
source: Therefore, transparent aposematic Lepidoptera benefit from a double protection from predation, which can act at different distances (Barnett et al., 2018; Cuthill, 2019; Tullberg et al., 2005): transparent aposematic species are less detectable than opaque species (McClure et al., 2019), but when detected they may be recognized as unpalatable by experienced predators, due to their aposematic wing pattern, and spared by those predators.
evidence: This is speculation based on the dual function of transparency and aposematism.

claim: Forked piliform scales have previously been reported in the highly transparent nymphalid species Greta oto.
source: Forked piliform scales have previously been reported in the highly transparent nymphalid species Greta oto (Binetti et al., 2009; Siddique et al., 2015), which belongs to the mimetic butterfly Ithomiini tribe.
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Erected scales have been previously reported in the riodinid Chorinea sylphina and in the nymphalid Parantica sita.
source: Erected scales (i.e. with a non-zero angle between the scale basis and the wing membrane) have been previously reported in the riodinid Chorinea sylphina (Dushkina et al., 2017) and in the nymphalid Parantica sita (Goodwyn et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Some species have coloured erected scales that are completely perpendicular to the wing membrane, such as in the ithomiine Methona curvifascia.
source: Here, we describe some species with coloured erected scales that are completely perpendicular to the wing membrane, such as in the ithomiine Methona curvifascia, and some species with transparent scales.
evidence: This is supported by the microscopy observations in this study.

claim: Some species have transparent scales.
source: Here, we describe some species with coloured erected scales that are completely perpendicular to the wing membrane, such as in the ithomiine Methona curvifascia, and some species with transparent scales.
evidence: This is supported by the microscopy observations in this study.

claim: Coloured erected scales and transparent scales were reported in transparent Lepidoptera only recently.
source: Both these features were reported in transparent Lepidoptera only recently (Gomez et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: Maze-like nanostructures have only been reported on the corneal surface of insect eyes.
source: While nipple arrays and pillars have previously been described on the wing of the sphingid Cephonodes hylas (Yoshida et al., 1997) and in the nymphalid Greta oto (Binetti et al., 2009; Siddique et al., 2015), respectively, maze-like nanostructures have only been reported on the corneal surface of insect eyes (Blagodatski et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: Sponge-like type of nanostructures is reported here for the first time.
source: Moreover, the sponge-like type of nanostructures is reported here for the first time.
evidence: This is a novel observation from the SEM imaging in this study.

claim: Pillars are a subcategory of nipple arrays, with higher and more densely packed nipples with enlarged bases.
source: Those nanostructures can be related to the classification proposed by Blagodatski et al., 2015: pillars are a subcategory of nipple arrays, with higher and more densely packed nipples with enlarged bases; sponge-like nanostructures are similar to dimples (holes embedded in a matrix), although with much bigger and more profound holes.
evidence: This is an inference based on comparison with the classification in cited literature.

claim: Sponge-like nanostructures are similar to dimples (holes embedded in a matrix), although with much bigger and more profound holes.
source: Those nanostructures can be related to the classification proposed by Blagodatski et al., 2015: pillars are a subcategory of nipple arrays, with higher and more densely packed nipples with enlarged bases; sponge-like nanostructures are similar to dimples (holes embedded in a matrix), although with much bigger and more profound holes.
evidence: This is an inference based on comparison with the classification in cited literature.

claim: Nipples, mazes and dimples have been found to be produced by Turing's reaction-diffusion models.
source: Nipples, mazes and dimples have been found to be produced by Turing's reaction-diffusion models, a solid framework that explains pattern formation in biology (Turing, 1952).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: Mean transmittance increases when membrane coverage decreases, either due to reduced scale surface and/or scale density.
source: To summarise, mean transmittance increases when membrane coverage decreases, either due to reduced scale surface and/or scale density, because there is less material interacting (reflecting, diffusing, or absorbing) with light.
evidence: This is an inference from the PGLS analyses linking structural features to mean transmittance.

claim: Light transmission is negatively correlated to light reflection.
source: Mean transmittance also increases when nanostructure density increases. Light transmission is indeed negatively correlated to light reflection and nanostructures are known to have anti-reflective properties, as demonstrated in the sphingid Cephonodes hylas (Yoshida et al., 1997) and in the nymphalid Greta oto (Siddique et al., 2015).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Nanostructures are known to have anti-reflective properties.
source: Mean transmittance also increases when nanostructure density increases. Light transmission is indeed negatively correlated to light reflection and nanostructures are known to have anti-reflective properties, as demonstrated in the sphingid Cephonodes hylas (Yoshida et al., 1997) and in the nymphalid Greta oto (Siddique et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Nanostructures create a gradient of refractive index between air and wing tissue.
source: Reflection increases as the difference in refractive index between air and organic materials increases. Nanostructures create a gradient of refractive index between air and wing tissue, and gradient efficiency in reducing reflection increases with a smooth increase in proportion of chitin inside the nanostructures.
evidence: This is established knowledge about how nanostructures reduce reflection.

claim: Pillars with conical bases are more effective at cancelling reflection than cylinders because cones produce a smoother air:chitin gradient from air to wing than cylinders.
source: For instance, pillars with conical bases are more effective at cancelling reflection than cylinders because cones produce a smoother air:chitin gradient from air to wing than cylinders (Siddique et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: Nanostructure density is highly correlated to nanostructure type.
source: In our case, nanostructure density is highly correlated to nanostructure type, which we have defined according to their shape (phylogenetic ANOVA on nanostructure density with nanostructure type as factor: F = 26.26, p-value = 0.001, see Supplementary file 3d and e for details).
evidence: This is supported by the phylogenetic ANOVA presented in Supplementary file 3d and e.

claim: The nanostructures whose shape likely creates the smoother gradient (pillar and sponge) are also the denser ones.
source: Specifically, the nanostructures whose shape likely creates the smoother gradient (pillar and sponge) are also the denser ones.
evidence: This is an inference from the correlation between nanostructure density and type.

claim: When nanostructure density increases, light reflection decreases.
source: When nanostructure density increases, light reflection thus decreases.
evidence: This is an inference from the anti-reflective properties of nanostructures.

claim: The chitin wing membrane only absorbs a small amount of light between 300 and 700 nm.
source: Light can either be transmitted, reflected or absorbed, and assuming that the chitin wing membrane only absorbs a small amount of light between 300 and 700 nm (Stavenga et al., 2014), when light reflection decreases because of the presence of nanostructures light transmission necessarily increases, which explains the positive effect of nanostructure density on mean transmittance.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: When light reflection decreases because of the presence of nanostructures, light transmission necessarily increases.
source: Light can either be transmitted, reflected or absorbed, and assuming that the chitin wing membrane only absorbs a small amount of light between 300 and 700 nm (Stavenga et al., 2014), when light reflection decreases because of the presence of nanostructures light transmission necessarily increases, which explains the positive effect of nanostructure density on mean transmittance.
evidence: This is an inference based on the physics of light and the properties of chitin.

claim: Thicker membranes, which contain more chitin, absorb more light than thinner ones, thereby reducing light transmission.
source: We showed that mean transmittance decreases when membrane thickness increases, because wing membrane is mainly made of chitin and even if chitin absorbs a little amount of light (Stavenga et al., 2014), thicker membranes, which contain more chitin, absorb more light than thinner ones, thereby reducing light transmission.
evidence: This is an inference based on the absorption properties of chitin.

claim: Wings covered with transparent scales transmit more light than wings covered with coloured scales due to the presence of pigments.
source: We finally showed, as Gomez et al., 2021, that wings covered with transparent scales transmit more light than wings covered with coloured scales. This is due to the presence of pigments, such as melanins or ommochromes commonly found in butterfly scales, which absorb some part of the light spectrum, thereby reducing light transmission.
evidence: This is an inference supported by a citation and knowledge about pigment absorption.

claim: Nanostructures are more labile than microstructures.
source: Our data suggest that nanostructures are more labile than microstructures.
evidence: This is an inference from the phylogenetic signal analyses showing weaker phylogenetic signal for nanostructures than microstructures.

claim: Nanostructures could evolve more readily in response to selection on the degree of transparency.
source: Nanostructures could therefore evolve more readily in response to selection on the degree of transparency.
evidence: This is speculation based on the greater lability of nanostructures.

claim: The presence and higher densities of nanostructures increase mean transmittance when scale density is already low, thereby allowing fine-tuning of transparency.
source: We showed that the presence and higher densities of nanostructures increase mean transmittance when scale density is already low, thereby allowing fine-tuning of transparency.
evidence: This is an inference from the interaction between scale density and nanostructure density in the PGLS models.

claim: The interplay between scales and nanostructures can modulate the degree of transparency.
source: The interplay between scales and nanostructures can thus modulate the degree of transparency and the selective pressures on the transmission properties of transparent patches may select specific associations of structural features.
evidence: This is an inference from the PGLS analyses showing effects of both scales and nanostructures on transmittance.

claim: Selective pressures on the transmission properties of transparent patches may select specific associations of structural features.
source: The interplay between scales and nanostructures can thus modulate the degree of transparency and the selective pressures on the transmission properties of transparent patches may select specific associations of structural features.
evidence: This is speculation based on the convergence of structural syndromes among co-mimics.

claim: Convergence of transparency features in aposematic mimetic Lepidoptera may be the result of selection by predators, likely through aposematism.
source: To conclude, this study reveals convergence of transparency features in aposematic mimetic Lepidoptera, which may be the result of selection by predators, likely through aposematism, even though transparent patches may also be under other local selection pressures such as selection for crypsis or adaptation to climatic conditions.
evidence: This is an inference from the convergence analyses, acknowledging alternative explanations.

claim: Transparent patches may also be under other local selection pressures such as selection for crypsis or adaptation to climatic conditions.
source: To conclude, this study reveals convergence of transparency features in aposematic mimetic Lepidoptera, which may be the result of selection by predators, likely through aposematism, even though transparent patches may also be under other local selection pressures such as selection for crypsis or adaptation to climatic conditions.
evidence: This is speculation acknowledging alternative selective pressures.

claim: Transparency entails strong structural modifications of scales that might impair other functions such as thermoregulation, hydrophobicity and perhaps mate signalling.
source: Transparency entails strong structural modifications of scales that might impair other functions such as thermoregulation (Berthier, 2005), hydrophobicity (Goodwyn et al., 2009) and perhaps mate signalling.
evidence: This is speculation supported by citations about scale functions.

claim: Transparency may come at a cost in large-winged insects.
source: Transparency may therefore come at a cost in those large-winged insects, which may explain why it is not pervasive among Lepidoptera.
evidence: This is speculation based on the potential functional trade-offs of transparency.

claim: The wing of the translucent papilionid Parnassius glacialis are less hydrophobic than most Lepidoptera wings.
source: Scales in Lepidoptera are not only involved in colour patterns but also play a role in hydrophobicity. The scale modifications underlying transparency described in our study may impair the waterproofing properties of wings, as shown by Goodwyn et al., 2009 the wing of the translucent papilionid Parnassius glacialis are less hydrophobic than most Lepidoptera wings.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: The scale modifications underlying transparency may impair the waterproofing properties of wings.
source: Scales in Lepidoptera are not only involved in colour patterns but also play a role in hydrophobicity. The scale modifications underlying transparency described in our study may impair the waterproofing properties of wings, as shown by Goodwyn et al., 2009 the wing of the translucent papilionid Parnassius glacialis are less hydrophobic than most Lepidoptera wings.
evidence: This is speculation supported by a citation showing reduced hydrophobicity in a transparent species.

claim: Across the 62 species, the mean transmittance ranges from 0.0284% in Eresia nauplius to 71.7% in Godyris panthyale.
source: Across the 62 species, the mean transmittance ranges from 0.0284 % in Eresia nauplius to 71.7 % in Godyris panthyale (mean: 29.2%, median: 31.6%, Supplementary file 1d).
evidence: This is supported by the spectrophotometry measurements presented in Supplementary file 1d.

claim: The physical property 'mean transmittance' is correlated to what is predicted to be perceived by predators based on vision modelling.
source: The physical property 'mean transmittance' (a proxy for the degree of transparency), is correlated to what is predicted to be perceived by predators based on vision modelling, (see Appendix and Supplementary file 3a–c for details), as shown in Gomez et al., 2021.
evidence: This is supported by analyses in the Appendix and Supplementary file 3a–c, and a citation.
